newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland prepares EU integration strategy.
newsitem.headline: Poland prepares EU integration strategy.

text.p: Poland on Thursday unveiled a strategic programme for integration with the European Union, which provides for further economic liberalisation to bring the country into the EU by the year 2002.

The scheme, called the National Integration Strategy, is a declaration that Poland will fully liberalise trade, its labour market, capital transactions and investment rules for the EU countries by the time it joins.

"We would like to start accession talks with the EU in early 1998, then there would be two to three years of negotiations and ...the year 2002 is a realistic date for our entry," Danuta Huebner, the secretary of the government's European Integration Committee said, presenting the programme.
Poland officially seeks to join the union by the year 2000 and has won French and German support for this goal, but Brussels officials say 2002 is the earliest practical date.

The programme, due to be adopted by the government this month and then sent to parliament for approval, also states that in a longer perspective Poland would strive to join the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU).

But Poland would need EU financial help in the pre-accession period to restructure some of its ailing industries and may ask to be allowed to protect them longer than envisaged by the country's EU association treaty, said Jaroslaw Pietras, the committee's senior director.
"We expect the union will create pre-accession funds...to help us with the task of restructuring," Pietras told the news conference.
He said agriculture and environment protection rules were among areas in which adjustment to EU standards would last longest.
Analysts say Poland's steel, mining, shipbuilding, oil and other heavy industries are also far from being able to compete with their Western counterparts without protection barriers.

The integration programe, which will be supplemented by many more concrete schemes over the next several years as the integration process proceeds, obliges the government to speedily adjust Poland's legal system to EU regulations.
"The scope of the task is perhaps even larger than that of our economic reforms during the early 1990s," said Pietras.

The programme also provides for a broad education campaign about the European Union, aimed at preserving its favourable image among Poles. Opinion polls show about 75 percent of Poles want to join the EU.
